578.title: Manipulator–Mechanism Design-II
578.notes: Lecture19 title and lecturer attribution only.
578.excluded: Title and attribution; no technical content.

579.title: Learning Outcome
579.notes: Five outcome bullets: redundant/closed chains, actuation/transmission/selection, stiffness/compliance, position/force sensing, mobile manipulation workspace/trajectory/kinematics.

580.title: Redundant & Closed-chain Structures - Micromanipulators
580.notes: Redundancy stated as more than six DOF for full spatial pose; closed loops; distal fast precise micromanipulator DOFs; extra joints help singularity/collision avoidance. The universal 6-DOF finite-solutions and 7-DOF infinite-solutions-for-any-pose claims require reachable regular poses, rank/task/limits qualifiers. Redundancy is task-relative, not always n>6.

581.title: Closed-loop structures
581.notes: Closed-loop versus serial topology; Motoman L-3 joints2/3 named; increased stiffness versus generally smaller joint range/workspace. Right schematic labels moving end-effector upper platform, base below and dashed closed-loop route; three drawn struts illustrate topology, not proof of six actuators or a Motoman L-3 image.

582.title: The Stewart Mechanism
582.notes: Six linear actuators connect base and moving platform; each leg base universal joint2DOF, platform spherical joint3DOF. Fully parallel6DOF, easy inverse length computation versus complex forward pose recovery, high stiffness/load capacity and limited workspace. Right photo shows actual six-leg platform. Inverse length derived as norm(p+Rbi−ai), not printed; “often no closed-form” not a categorical impossibility.

583.title: Grübler’s Formula
583.notes: Exact formula F=6(l−n−1)+Σ fi. l counts links including ground; n counts joints. Counts six universal2DOF, six spherical3DOF, six prismatic1DOF, n18. The formula assumes independent generic constraints; singular/special overconstrained cases need rank analysis. Photo repeats the platform, no new dimensions.

584.title: Stewart Mechanism Example (Continued)
584.notes: Twelve actuator links (two rigid members per telescoping actuator), one base, one platform =>l14. Sum fi12+18+6=36. F=6(14−18−1)+36=6. Continued photo no new geometry; numerical derivation is substantive incremental content.

585.title: Actuation Schemes - Actuator location
585.notes: Integrated motor, reducer and transmission design; effects on dynamic performance, control and structure. Local direct drive: actuator at/near joint output attached directly; remote drive toward base away from driven joint. Proximity alone is not sufficient to call a geared motor direct drive; use stated direct-output connection.

586.title: Reduction and transmission systems
586.notes: Spur, bevel, worm, cross-helical gears named and pictured (photos are unlabelled individually); backlash/friction; tighter mesh trades less backlash for more friction. η>1 is speed-reduction ratio, not efficiency. ωo=ωi/η and τo=ητi require ideal lossless magnitudes or consistent sign convention; actual friction acknowledged above makes unconditional exact torque equation incomplete.

587.title: Flexible Bands, Cables, and Belts
587.notes: Remote transmission and possible reduction; flexibility proportional to element length under unchanged material/section; tension-only requires preload or opposing active drive. Toothed belts and roller chains described as stiffer/compact, chains around smaller pulleys (qualitative comparisons need fixed design basis). Diagram small input r1 left, larger output r2 right, open belt; η=r2/r1, no slip implied, opposite ratio would be speedup.

588.title: Lead Screws and Ball-Bearing Screws
588.notes: Rotary-to-linear conversion. Left drawing direct lead-screw/nut thread contact labelled Nut; right drawing balls between threads labelled Race. Lead screws stiff/high load/high friction; ball screw recirculating bearings reduce friction and are typically backdrivable, not always self-locking. No lead/pitch equation printed; derived kinematics only if explicitly supplied.

589.title: Stiffness and Deflections
589.notes: Structural and drivetrain stiffness important. Source says most industrial robots infer tool pose via forward kinematics of sensed joint positions; do not present survey claim as timeless fact. Compliance yields sag under gravity/load and rigid-model pose error; flexibility produces resonances limiting dynamic performance/control bandwidth. Encoders alone may miss unmodelled link deformation.

590.title: Flexible elements in parallel and series
590.notes: Parallel k=k1+k2; series1/k=1/k1+1/k2; compliance reciprocal. For reduction stages in series, stiffness/compliance must first be referred to the same coordinate/shaft using p592; raw numbers on different shafts cannot be directly summed. Scalar linear-spring model, positive k, common generalized coordinate.

591.title: Stiffness and Deflections – Shafts and Gears
591.notes: Solid round shaft torsional k=Gπd^4/(32l), d diameter not radius, l length G shear modulus. Gear output stiffness with input fixed k=Cg b r², b face width r output radius Cg material constant. Both rotational units N·m/rad, not N/m. Shaft and gear photos contain no dimensions; avoid inferring tooth counts. Formula assumes uniform linear-elastic solid shaft; hollow shaft needs polar difference not supplied.

592.title: Stiffness and Deflections Belts and Links
592.notes: Exact equations ko=η²ki for ideal reduction η>1; belt axial k=AE/l; hollow round cantilever end-load stiffness3πE(do^4−di^4)/(64l³); hollow square E(wo^4−wi^4)/(4l³). Belt schematic right; cantilever clamped left with downward tip-region load. Distinguish rotational transformed k from translational belt/beam k. Assumptions small linear elastic deflection, constant section, correct end-load boundary; do>di>=0, wo>wi>=0. Formulas check as3EI/l³.

593.title: Electric Motors
593.notes: Electric motors easy interface/precision; qualitative power-weight comparison with fluids; DC brushed motor stationary brushes feed rotor windings through rotating commutator. Winding overheating major limit; torque proportional current for constant flux/linear model. Generic motor cutaway at upper right does not explicitly show labelled brushes/commutator, so do not identify DC topology from photo alone.

594.title: Position Sensing
594.notes: Servo control uses desired-minus-sensed joint position error to generate force/torque command. Co-located sensor at actuator shaft is recommended. “Most effective” not a universal end-effector-accuracy guarantee; shaft sensing can miss downstream compliance p589. No sensor hardware diagram. Modern-industry prevalence claims should be source-attributed.

595.title: Force Sensing
595.notes: Strain-gauge contact force sensors: bonded to metal, output proportional strain in calibrated range. Design count/placement/stiffness/sensitivity/overload; positions actuator/wrist/fingertips; wrist3–6 wrench components. Photo shows cylindrical transducer and enlarged serpentine bonded foil gauge with two leads; do not infer total gauge count or six-axis capability from one pictured gauge. Not all possible force sensors use gauges; scope to illustrated class.

596.title: Force Sensor Design Issues
596.notes: Flexure deflection creates stiffness-versus-sensitivity tradeoff; limit stops protect overload; minimizing welded/bolted joints near flexures reduces hysteresis (does not prove eliminates all hysteresis). Differential measurements improve linearity and reject shared temperature/off-axis effects under suitable arrangement, not all arbitrary differential pairs. Foil more durable/lower sensitivity; semiconductor higher sensitivity/more overload vulnerability; comparison as given.

597.title: Mobile Robots
597.notes: Interdisciplinary mechanical/electrical/electronics/computer/cognitive/social sciences; autonomous mobility focus versus fixed arms; multiple competence layers; kinematics, signal analysis, information theory, AI, probability. Small four-wheel top-view schematic no dimensions or drive labels. Do not identify drive type from icon alone, or define every mobile robot as necessarily unsupervised.

598.title: Locomotion
598.notes: Locomotion moves robot by forces against environment; source contrasts fixed-arm object manipulation. Legged locomotion uses articulated limbs and gait leg-lift/release sequence; differential/synchro/omnidirectional wheel drive names. Active COM shift may enable obstacle climbing beyond wheel size, not unconditional numerical guarantee. Drawings show biped stick figure and generic four-wheel icon, no detailed drive geometry.

599.title: Wheeled Mobile Robots
599.notes: Wheels efficient on flat ground and mechanically simple; general all-wheels-contact design and lower balance emphasis, not universal. Three wheels typically suffice for static stability only with noncollinear supports and COM projection inside support polygon; slope/dynamic forces can change result. Design focus traction/stability/maneuverability/control. Photo has four wheels and payload; no kinematic drive identification justified.

600.title: Wheel Geometry
600.notes: Wheel type plus arrangement determine wheel geometry and influence stability, maneuverability, controllability. No universally ideal configuration; choose based on environment/task constraints. Repeats some p599 ideas but adds explicit no-single-optimum application-specific tradeoff.

601.title: Mobile Robot Workspace and Degrees of Freedom
601.notes: Workspace is attainable poses; planar chassis coordinates x,y,theta in global frame; exactly three rigid planar pose DOFs independent of internal joint count. Do not equate three configuration coordinates to three independently commandable instantaneous velocities for nonholonomic wheels. Right ellipse labelled Environment (word linebreak cosmetic), car icon and star obstacles; not all drawn region necessarily collision-free or reachable.

602.title: Mobile Manipulation
602.notes: Arm mounted on mobile chassis extends reach; chassis gross motion versus arm fine tasks. Illustrated arm with gripper mounted on blue wheeled base; no exact DOF count justified by stylized joints/two visible wheels. Contrast of fixed-arm manipulation versus robot locomotion is illustrative, not a ban on simultaneous mobile manipulation.

603.title: Summary
603.notes: Integrated actuation/transmission/sensing/stiffness/control. Adds explicit autonomy modules locomotion, perception, localization, cognition, navigation and effective mobile design base selection, stability management, configuration-space planning. Not merely excluded summary: these named topics need coverage. Mobile base plus arm expands workspace/flexibility but obstacles/limits remain.
